content: For each ear, there is a eustachian tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the throat. This tube is responsible for draining fluid that is normally produced in the middle ear. If the eustachian tube becomes blocked, fluid can accumulate in the middle ear. When this occurs, microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses can proliferate, leading to an infection. Ear infections are particularly common in infants and children, partly because their eustachian tubes are more prone to becoming clogged. While ear infections can also occur in adults, they are less frequent compared to children. The most common bacterial causes of otitis media are Streptococcus pneumoniae and nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae. Dysfunction of the eustachian tube can impair the clearance of bacteria from the middle ear, increasing the risk of infection. In older adolescents and young adults, Haemophilus influenzae was historically a leading cause of ear infections during their childhood. The impact of the anti-Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine, which is routinely administered to children, on the patterns of ear infections remains unclear. This is because the vaccine is only effective against serotype b strains, which rarely cause otitis media. In addition to Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, the common cold is another significant contributor to otitis media. Colds indirectly lead to many cases of otitis media by compromising the normal defenses of the epithelial cells in the upper respiratory tract. Another common bacterial cause of otitis media is Moraxella catarrhalis, a gram-negative, aerobic, oxidase-positive diplococcus. Less commonly, otitis media can be caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Any condition that causes the eustachian tubes to become swollen or blocked can result in fluid accumulation in the middle ear behind the eardrum. These conditions include: Allergies Colds and sinus infections Excess mucus and saliva production during teething Infected or enlarged adenoids Exposure to tobacco smoke or other irritants Children who frequently drink from a sippy cup or bottle while lying on their back are also at increased risk of developing ear infections. Contrary to popular belief, getting water in the ears does not cause acute ear infections unless the eardrum has a perforation from a previous episode. Ear infections are most common during the winter months. While ear infections themselves are not contagious, colds can spread among children and may lead to ear infections in some of them.
